title: "Why posterior computation is necessary"

  enabled: true

On the [preceding page](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#a-robust-location-scale-model),
we constructed a posterior distribution for the parameters of a passage-level
Student-$t$ model. We could evaluate the prior times the likelihood at any
particular pair $(\mu,\sigma)$, and a fine grid let us see which pairs received
more posterior density. But evaluating a posterior at a point is not usually
the final aim. We want to calculate quantities such as

$$
\mathbb{P}(\mu>0\mid\mathbf y),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\exp(\mu)\mid\mathbf y],
$$

or an interval containing a specified amount of posterior probability. Each
quantity requires us to combine information across the entire posterior
distribution.

Okay. So how do we actually do that combining?

For the two-parameter model, we already know one answer. We place a grid over
$(\mu,\log\sigma)$, evaluate the posterior kernel at every grid point,
normalize the resulting values so that they sum to one, and compute a weighted
sum. The problem is that this procedure becomes unusable surprisingly
quickly. If we put 300 grid points along each of two dimensions, we evaluate
$300^2=90{,}000$ parameter combinations. Ten dimensions would require
$300^{10}$ combinations. Adding parameters thus makes the grid grow far more
quickly than our ability to evaluate it.

We will call this the **posterior computation problem**: we can write down a
posterior kernel, but we cannot obtain the posterior summaries we want by
enumerating all relevant parameter values. The word *kernel* here means a
function proportional to the posterior density. As we saw in the discussion
of the [missing normalizing constant](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#the-missing-normalizer),
the kernel contains the prior and likelihood terms that vary with the
parameters while leaving out one common constant.

The basic idea in this part of the course is to replace an impossible sum over
all parameter values with a manageable average over carefully generated
parameter values. Getting from that idea to a reliable posterior analysis
will require us to answer three questions:

1. Which average would equal the posterior quantity if we could generate the
   right values?
2. How can we generate values whose long-run distribution is the posterior?
3. How can we tell whether a finite computer run gives an accurate enough
   approximation?

The first question leads to Monte Carlo integration. The second leads to
Markov chains, Metropolis--Hastings sampling, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and the
No-U-Turn Sampler. The third leads to trace plots, $\widehat R$, effective
sample size, and the HMC-specific diagnostic called a divergent transition.
We will work through these questions in that order.

## From a weighted grid to an expectation

Suppose, for the moment, that a posterior grid contains only four possible
values of $\mu$:

| value of $\mu$ | posterior probability | $\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$ |
|---:|---:|---:|
| $-0.03$ | $0.10$ | $0$ |
| $-0.01$ | $0.20$ | $0$ |
| $0.01$ | $0.40$ | $1$ |
| $0.03$ | $0.30$ | $1$ |

The indicator $\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$ equals one when its condition is true and
zero when its condition is false. We can calculate the posterior probability
that $\mu$ is positive by taking a weighted sum of that indicator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\mu>0\mid\mathbf y)
&=
(0)(0.10)+(0)(0.20)+(1)(0.40)+(1)(0.30)\\
&=0.70.
\end{aligned}
$$

Nothing mysterious has happened. We asked a yes-or-no question at each grid
point and then added the posterior probability assigned to the points where
the answer was yes.

Now suppose we want the posterior mean of $\mu$. We use the same posterior
probabilities but replace the indicator with the value of $\mu$ itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\mu\mid\mathbf y]
&=
(-0.03)(0.10)+(-0.01)(0.20)\\
&\quad +(0.01)(0.40)+(0.03)(0.30)\\ % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
&=0.008.
\end{aligned}
$$

These two calculations have the same form. We choose a function $g$ that
represents the posterior question and average $g(\mu)$ using the posterior
probabilities as weights. For the directional probability,
$g(\mu)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$. For the posterior mean, $g(\mu)=\mu$. And for the
geometric-scale duration ratio, $g(\mu)=\exp(\mu)$.

The [expected-value chapter](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd)
introduced exactly this operation for a random variable. Here we apply it to
a parameter after conditioning on the observed data:

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(\mu)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\sum_m g(\mu_m)\,
\mathbb{P}(\mu=\mu_m\mid\mathbf y).
$$

For a continuous parameter, individual points have probability zero, so a
weighted sum over points becomes an integral over short intervals:

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(\mu)\mid\mathbf y]
=
\int g(\mu)f(\mu\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\mu.
$$

The integral is thus the continuous version of the four-row calculation. The
factor $f(\mu\mid\mathbf y)\,\mathrm d\mu$ supplies the approximate posterior
probability in a very short interval around $\mu$, and $g(\mu)$ supplies the
quantity being averaged there. We will return to this connection on the
[Monte Carlo integration page](monte-carlo-integration.qmd#from-a-weighted-sum-to-a-draw-average).

## Replacing weights with repeated values

There is another way to reproduce the four-row calculation. Imagine drawing
100 values from the toy posterior. We would expect about 10 copies of $-0.03$,
20 copies of $-0.01$, 40 copies of $0.01$, and 30 copies of $0.03$. If those
counts occurred exactly, the ordinary mean of the 100 drawn values would be

$$
\frac{
10(-0.03)+20(-0.01)+40(0.01)+30(0.03)
}{100}
=0.008.
$$

The posterior weights have not disappeared. They have been represented by
how often each value occurs in the draws. Values with more posterior
probability appear more often, so an unweighted average over the draws
reproduces the weighted average over the grid.

This observation is the central computational move. If
$\mu^{(1)},\ldots,\mu^{(S)}$ are draws from the posterior, then

$$
\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S g(\mu^{(s)})
$$

approximates $\mathbb{E}[g(\mu)\mid\mathbf y]$. The approximation will vary
slightly when we repeat the simulation because a finite collection of random
draws will not contain the posterior values in exactly their expected
proportions. We will call that variation **Monte Carlo error** and derive a
standard error for it on the next page.

A potential worry is that this sounds circular. We wanted the posterior
summary because the posterior was hard to normalize, and now we are assuming
that we can draw from the posterior. That worry is exactly right. Direct
posterior draws are available for some simple distributions, but they are not
available for most models we actually want to fit. The pages in this section
develop progressively more general ways around that obstacle.

## The sequence of computational ideas

It will help to keep one question in view as the algorithms become more
elaborate: *How does this method make frequently occurring parameter values
line up with posterior probability?*

| Method | Values we can generate | How posterior probability enters |
|---|---|---|
| [Monte Carlo integration](monte-carlo-integration.qmd) | independent draws from the posterior | high-probability values occur more often |
| [Importance sampling](importance-sampling.qmd) | independent draws from an easier distribution | a density ratio corrects how often values occurred |
| [Markov chain Monte Carlo](markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd) | dependent states from a transition rule | the rule is constructed so that the posterior is its stationary distribution |
| [Metropolis--Hastings](metropolis-hastings.qmd) | proposed moves from the current state | an acceptance probability corrects the proposed flow between regions |
| [Hamiltonian Monte Carlo](hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd) | gradient-guided trajectories | a final acceptance step corrects numerical trajectory error |
| [The No-U-Turn Sampler](no-u-turn-sampler.qmd) | adaptively extended HMC trajectories | the path stops before it doubles back and one valid state is retained |

The algorithms do not define different posteriors. They are different ways
of approximating the same posterior target. If two correct methods are run
long enough and accurately enough, they should agree on posterior summaries
up to their remaining numerical error.

This gives us a useful separation. The prior and likelihood determine which
parameter values receive posterior support. The computational algorithm
determines how we explore and summarize that support. Increasing the number
of simulation iterations may reduce numerical error, but it leaves the data,
likelihood, and prior unchanged.

## What the diagnostics are trying to establish

Once we use a Markov chain, our generated values will be dependent: the next
state is constructed from the current state. Dependence does not prevent us
from estimating posterior expectations, but it creates two practical
questions.

First, did the chains reach and explore the same posterior distribution? We
will inspect their paths with [trace and rank plots](checking-markov-chains.qmd)
and quantify cross-chain agreement with
[$\widehat R$](rhat.qmd). Second, how much numerical information did the
dependent draws provide? We will describe within-chain dependence using
[autocorrelation](autocorrelation.qmd) and translate that dependence into an
[effective sample size](effective-sample-size.qmd).

HMC adds a third question because its trajectories are calculated
numerically. Did the numerical integrator follow the posterior geometry
accurately? [Divergent transitions](divergent-transitions.qmd) warn us about
large integration errors, and [parameter-pair plots](parameter-pair-plots.qmd)
help locate the part of the joint posterior where those errors occurred.

None of these diagnostics asks whether the statistical model gives a useful
account of the linguistic data. Once we have evidence that the computation
worked, we still need to generate the observations predicted by the fitted
model and compare them with the observations we actually saw. The
[generated-quantities](generated-quantities.qmd) and
[posterior-predictive-check](posterior-predictive-checks.qmd) pages carry out
that return to the data.

## Recap and forward link

1. The posterior computation problem arises because the summaries we want
   combine information across a posterior that we cannot enumerate on a grid.
2. A posterior summary can be written as the expectation of a function $g$;
   different choices of $g$ answer different posterior questions.
3. Draw frequency can stand in for posterior weight, which turns a weighted
   sum or integral into an ordinary average over draws.
4. Sampling diagnostics evaluate the numerical approximation. Posterior
   predictive checks evaluate selected consequences of the statistical model.

The [Monte Carlo integration page](monte-carlo-integration.qmd#from-a-weighted-sum-to-a-draw-average)
now derives the draw average and its numerical standard error.

## Check your understanding

1. Which function $g(\mu)$ turns a posterior expectation into
   $\mathbb{P}(\mu>0\mid\mathbf y)$?
2. Why does an ordinary average over posterior draws reproduce a
   posterior-weighted average?
3. Which part of an analysis changes when we increase the number of retained
   simulation draws?
4. Why do we need model checks after all sampling diagnostics look good?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Use $g(\mu)=\mathbf 1\{\mu>0\}$, which is one for positive values and zero
   otherwise. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Values occur among the draws in proportion to their posterior probability,
   so their frequency supplies the weight. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The numerical approximation changes. The data, prior, likelihood, and
   posterior target remain fixed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A sampler can approximate the declared posterior accurately even when the
   declared model fails to reproduce a scientifically relevant feature of the
   observations. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
